results.title: Patient-specific uncertainty calibration of deep learning-based autosegmentation networks for adaptive MRI-guided lung radiotherapy - IOPscience
results.content: To obtain individual single-label patient-specific models for each OAR and the GTV (PS; see figure 1(c)), we followed the approach described by Kawula *et al* Briefly summarized, network weights were initialized from the BM and then further trained on the patient’s planning image and contour, adjusting all parameters, with data augmentation applied to avoid overfitting. The uncertainty calibration of the OAR- or GTV-specific BM and PS models for each fraction image of each test patient was individually evaluated using reliability diagrams (Degroot and Fienberg 1983) and quantified through the expected calibration error (ECE), a standard scalar metric in machine learning to evaluate the discrepancy between predicted confidence levels and actual accuracy (Degroot and Fienberg 1983, Naeini *et al* 2015, Guo *et al* 2017, Nixon *et al* 2019). The reliability diagrams were constructed and the ECE values were calculated this way for all fraction images of the test patients for the MCD maps obtained by the BM or PS models for each OAR and the GTV. To illustrate the effects of patient-specific model fine-tuning and uncertainty calibration on the models’ outputs, a fraction image, clinical contours, model predictions, and predicted probability levels at 20% and 80% are presented in in figures 4–6. By both uncertainty calibration (calBM and calPS) and patient-specific fine-tuning (PS and calPS), additional slices in cranial direction were included in the predicted masks, leading to reduced HD95 values of 5–8 mm for these model variants. Post-training uncertainty calibration shifted the predicted probability values of voxels with high confidence toward greater uncertainty (i.e. closer to a predicted probability of 0.5; visible in the histograms in the last column), resulting in increased relOU values: from 11% (BM) to 25% (calBM) for the population-based models and from 8.5% (PS) to 18% (calPS) for the patient-specific fine-tuned models. The reduction in HD95 values was particularly strong for the tubular OARs, as patient-specific fine-tuning enabled the models to adapt the contour length based on the planning contour, resulting in improved segmentation performance on the fraction MRIs. In terms of uncertainty metrics, for all OARs, uncertainty calibration led to an increase in the median relOU values by a factor of 1.1–2.8 across all test patients, for both the population-based and fine-tuned models.

results.content: More speciﬁcally it evaluates diﬀerent estimators of the Expected Calibration Error (ECE), amongst which legacy estimators and some novel ones, proposed in this paper. We ﬁnally assess in Section 5 the relevance of legacy and proposed estimators empirically using a broad empirical setup.1 2 Context and Related Work The oldest attempt to quantify calibration has been the reliability diagram [3,11] for binary classiﬁcation. Mirroring the procedure used to compute the reliability diagram, the empirical Expected Calibration Error (ECE) was designed [3], and later has been proven to be an estimator for the natural the-oretical notion of calibration error [4]. Recent works mostly rely on the binning based legacy estimator of the ECE to quantify calibration. More recently [7] made clearer the notion of calibration for multiclass classiﬁers, and new estimators of the ECE with adaptive binning have been proposed in [12] along side with uncertainty aware reliability diagrams [1]. In this context we aim at improving the evaluation of calibration in the setting of classiﬁcation, and speciﬁcally focus on estimators of the ECE as the theoretical deﬁnition itself has been consistently adopted. To build the reliability diagram (in the binary setting), a uniform binning scheme (the [0, 1] interval is split into equal bins) is used, and each holdout sample is mapped into a bin based on the score given by the model for the positive class (procedure deﬁned below as 1-bin mapping). The main beneﬁt this proposed notion of local calibration error oﬀers is its usability in practice to know the uncertainty of a model on a speciﬁc score, which cannot be evaluated with enough precision using previous tools (points in a reliability diagram can be used for an interpolation aiming at the same result, yet the precision of such procedure is very low, and interpolation at that scale is questionable). This idea, illustrated on Figure 1 (right), allows the prediction of conﬁdence intervals for the class probabilities instead of point estimates, by only looking at the uncertainty on the bootstrapped reliability curve at the score output by the model. Estimating Expected Calibration Errors 11 For the class-wise setting, there is no clear outperformer in all data regimes among the tested estimators.

results.content: # uncertainty-calibration 0.1.4. Utilities to calibrate model uncertainties and measure calibration. # Uncertainty Calibration Library. This repository contains library code to measure the calibration error of models, including confidence intervals computed by Bootstrap resampling, and code to recalibrate models. Our functions estimate the calibration error and ECE more accurately than prior "plugin" estimators and we provide Bootstrap confidence intervals. See Verified Uncertainty Calibration for more details. Motivating example for uncertainty calibration: Calster and Vickers 2015 train a random forest that takes in features such as tumor size and presence of teratoma, and tries to predict the probability a patient has testicular cancer. Calibration is a popular way to measure the quality of a model's uncertainties, and recalibration is a way to take an existing model and correct its uncertainties to make them better. This library focuses on calibration for classification tasks. Measuring the calibration error of a model is as simple as:. Our library makes it very easy to measure confidence intervals on the calibration error as well, using bootstrap resamples. ## Advanced: ECE, Debiasing, and Top-Label Calibration Error. By default, our library measure per-class, root-mean-squared calibration error, and uses the techniques in Verified Uncertainty Calibration to accurately estimate the calibration error. However, we also support measuring the ECE (Guo et al) and using older, less accurate, ways of estimating the calibration error. get_top_calibration_error(model_probs, labels, p = 1). Multiclass calibration vs ECE / Top-label: When measuring the calibration error of a multiclass model, we can measure the calibration error of all classes (per-class calibration error), or of the top prediction. ## Verified Uncertainty Calibration paper. This repository also contains code for the NeurIPS 2019 (Spotlight) paper Verified Uncertainty Calibration. * The calibration error of methods like Platt scaling and temperature scaling are typically underestimated, and cannot be easily measured. * We propose an efficient recalibration method where the calibration error can be measured. * Experiments showing the debiased estimator can estimate calibration error with fewer samples than standard estimator (Section 5) Running each experiment saves plots in the corresponding folder in saved\_files. uncertainty-calibration-0..gz (15.9 kB view details). results.content: We learn this Uncertainty-aware Attention (UA) mechanism using variational inference, and validate it on various risk prediction tasks from electronic health records on which our model signiﬁcantly outperforms existing attention models. For further validation on prediction reliability, we evaluate it for the uncertainty calibration performance, and prediction under the scenario where the model can defer the decision by saying “I don’t know”, whose results show that UA yields signiﬁcantly better calibrated networks that can better avoid making incorrect predictions on instances that it is uncertain, compared to baseline attention models.
